h1: Serving wine at the right temperature in an Indian summer
title: Wine Serving Temperature in India | Craft Beer School
desc: The right serving temperature for sparkling, white, rose and red wine, plus how to get there when the room is 32 °C.
teaser: Room temperature for red wine meant a cool European cellar, not a Delhi flat in May. Here is how to fix it.
standfirst: Temperature changes how a wine tastes more than almost anything else you control at home. In an Indian summer, nearly every wine is served too warm. A fridge, an ice bucket and a few minutes of planning put it right.
sections:
Warmth makes alcohol and aroma evaporate faster. A little warmth helps a red wine smell of fruit. Too much and the alcohol takes over, so the wine smells hot and tastes soupy. Cold does the opposite. It mutes aroma, sharpens acidity and makes tannin feel harder.

That is why the right temperature depends on the wine. Light, crisp wines are built on freshness and acidity, so they are served cold. Big reds are built on fruit and texture, so they are served cooler than a room but warmer than a fridge.

• Sparkling wine: 6 to 10 °C. Colder for simple fizz, a touch warmer for complex vintage sparkling.
  • Light, crisp whites and rosé such as Sauvignon Blanc: 7 to 10 °C.
  • Fuller whites such as oaked Chardonnay or Viognier: 10 to 13 °C.
  • Light reds such as Pinot Noir or a young Zinfandel: 12 to 14 °C.
  • Full reds such as Cabernet Sauvignon or Shiraz: 15 to 18 °C.
  • Sweet wines and port: sweet whites cold at 6 to 10 °C, port around 16 °C.

A home fridge runs at about 4 °C, so a white straight from the fridge is a little too cold. That is the safe side to be on. It will warm in the glass in a few minutes.
Room temperature is a European idea

The old advice to serve red wine at room temperature comes from houses in France and England where a room might be 16 to 18 °C. In much of India a room in summer is 30 °C or more. A red served at that temperature tastes flat and boozy, which is why so many people think they do not like red wine.

The fix is simple: put red wine in the fridge for 20 to 30 minutes before you open it. It will come out at around 16 °C and warm in the glass. In a hot room or on a terrace, put the bottle back in the fridge or a cool bucket between glasses. The same thinking applies to beer, as our guide to beer serving temperature shows.

The quickest way to chill a bottle is an ice bucket filled with half ice and half water. Water touches the whole bottle, so it cools far faster than ice alone. Add a good handful of salt and it gets colder still. A white wine will drop to drinking temperature in about 15 to 20 minutes.

The freezer works too, but set a timer. A forgotten bottle can freeze, push out its cork or crack. A wet cloth wrapped round the bottle in the freezer speeds it up a little.

Ice cubes in wine are frowned on because they water it down. With a simple rosé on a hot afternoon, a cube or two is a practical choice. Just do not do it to a wine you paid a lot for.
Keeping it at the right temperature

In Indian heat the wine in your glass warms by several degrees within ten minutes. Pour smaller amounts and top up more often. Hold the glass by the stem so your hand does not warm the bowl. Keep the bottle in the bucket between pours, but lift reds out once they feel cold to the touch.

Storage matters before any of this. Wine kept in a hot cupboard or a car boot ages fast and goes stale. If you buy wine to keep for a few weeks, store it lying down in the coolest, darkest part of the house, away from the kitchen. Our guide on wine storage and the cold chain in India covers what happens to wine before it reaches you.

The best way to learn this is to try it. Pour one glass of red straight from a warm shelf and another after 25 minutes in the fridge. Taste them side by side. Most people are surprised how much fruit appears in the cooler glass and how much harsh alcohol disappears.

Do the same with a white straight from the fridge and after ten minutes on the table. You will find the point where the aroma opens up and the wine still tastes fresh. That point is your serving temperature. It may not match any chart exactly.
faqs: What temperature should red wine be served at in India?
Light reds at about 12 to 14 °C and fuller reds at 15 to 18 °C. In a warm Indian room, 20 to 30 minutes in the fridge before opening gets you close.
How cold should white wine be?
Crisp whites at about 7 to 10 °C and fuller whites at 10 to 13 °C. Straight from a home fridge is slightly too cold. It warms quickly in the glass.
What is the fastest way to chill wine?
An ice bucket filled with half ice and half water, plus a handful of salt. A bottle reaches drinking temperature in about 15 to 20 minutes.
Is it wrong to put ice in wine?
It dilutes the wine, so avoid it with good bottles. With a simple rosé on a hot day, it is a practical choice.
